questions.stem: A surgeon decides how much to disclose by asking what a typical surgeon would tell patients about this operation. Which disclosure standard is this, and what is its main weakness?

options.A: Reasonable patient standard; hardest to apply because it must be tailored to each patient
options.B: Subjective standard; it focuses on the physician rather than the patient
options.C: Reasonable patient standard; it focuses on the physician rather than the patient
options.D: Reasonable physician standard; it focuses on the physician rather than the patient
options.E: Reasonable physician standard; hardest to apply because it must be tailored to each patient

questions.explanation: The reasonable physician standard asks what a typical physician would say; it is considered inconsistent with the goals of informed consent because it centers on the physician, not on what the patient needs to know. A, E: Tailoring to each patient is the subjective standard, the most challenging to practice. B: The subjective standard centers on this particular patient. C: The reasonable patient standard asks what the average patient needs to know.

questions.stem: An unconscious 45-year-old man in shock is brought to the emergency department with an intestinal perforation. No relatives or surrogate can be reached, and the surgeon judges that delay will be fatal. What is the appropriate basis for operating?

options.A: Presumed (implied) consent for an emergency intervention that prevents death
options.B: A general consent form signed at admission covers the surgery
options.C: The patient's presence in the hospital implies consent to treatment
options.D: A court order must be obtained before any surgery
options.E: Surgery must wait until the patient regains consciousness

questions.explanation: Presumed/implied consent applies only in emergencies when the patient is unconscious or incompetent, no surrogate is available, and the intervention prevents death or disability; a surgeon who acts with due care in good faith is not held responsible for an unfavourable outcome. B: Surgery and anesthesia require their own specific signed consent. C: Presence in the ward, ICU or clinic is not implied consent to all treatment. D, E: Delay would harm the patient; neither is required in a life-threatening emergency.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis agrees in the morning to a feeding tube. That evening she is disoriented and refuses it. The next morning she is lucid again and agrees, but cannot recall the evening. What should the team do?

options.A: Honor the evening refusal, since it is her most recent decision
options.B: Ask the court to appoint a guardian before proceeding
options.C: Place the tube, honoring the consistent decision made while lucid
options.D: Let her family decide, since her capacity varies
options.E: Postpone the procedure until she never shows confusion

questions.explanation: Decision-making capacity can vary with disease and medications; capacity is assessed during lucid periods, and a decision made consistently and persistently over time is honored. A: The refusal was made while disoriented. B: A court-appointed guardian is a rare last resort when no surrogate exists. D: She has capacity when lucid, so she decides. E: Unnecessary delay; her lucid decision is consistent.

questions.stem: Which practice meets the lecture's requirements for documenting informed consent before surgery?

options.A: A standard hospital form, signed by the patient, used for every procedure
options.B: A form signed routinely by the patient after a staff member points to the signature line
options.C: Verbal agreement recorded by the surgeon in the operative note
options.D: A form signed by the patient only, kept in the surgeon's office
options.E: A form in duplicate, signed by patient, doctor and an independent witness

questions.explanation: Consent should be dated, prepared in duplicate (a copy goes to the patient), signed by the patient or guardian, the doctor and an independent witness, and kept in the medical record. A: Consent is person- and procedure-specific; there is no standard form. B: Consent cannot be a signature on a dotted line obtained routinely by staff. C: Surgery and anesthesia usually require a signed form. D: The doctor and a witness must also sign, and it belongs in the patient's medical record.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her school teacher after a serious injury. Her parents and guardians cannot be reached. According to the lecture, from whom is consent obtained?

options.B: The teacher who brought the child
options.C: A judge, through a court order
options.E: No one until the parents are reached

questions.explanation: For children in an emergency when parents or guardians are unavailable, consent is taken from the person who brought the child, such as a school teacher. A: Children lack decision-making capacity to give consent, though their assent is sought when possible. C: Courts are for unresolved disputes or when no surrogate can be found. D: Not a listed decision-maker. E: Waiting would harm the child in an emergency.

questions.stem: Which Lebanese law governs patients' rights and informed consent?
questions.explanation: Law No. 574 of 2004 is the Lebanese law on Patients' Rights and Informed Consent. A: Human tissue and organ transplantation. B: Genetic tests. D: Implements the 1983 organ transplantation decree-law. E: Established the Lebanese National Consultative Committee on Ethics.
questions.source: Informed Consent, slide 16; Laws in Bioethics, slides 9–10
